By Coulomb's law the magnitude of the force between two point charges in air is \(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}\), with \(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2}\).

Converting the separation to SI units, \(r = 30\,\text{cm} = 0.30\,\text{m}\).

Substituting \(q_1 = 2 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\) and \(q_2 = 3 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\),

\(F = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2})(2 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C})(3 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C})}{(0.30\,\text{m})^{2}} = \dfrac{5.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{N m}^{2}}{9.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}}\)

\(F = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N}\)

Both charges are positive, so the force is repulsive and acts along the line joining the two spheres.

Force \(= 6.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N}\), repulsive.

Converting to SI units, \(q_1 = 0.4\,\mu\text{C} = 4 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\) and \(q_2 = -0.8\,\mu\text{C} = -8 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\), and the given force has magnitude \(F = 0.2\,\text{N}\).

(a) Coulomb's law gives \(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^{2}}\), so

\(r^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{F} = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2})(4 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C})(8 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C})}{0.2\,\text{N}}\)

\(r^{2} = \dfrac{2.88 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N m}^{2}}{0.2\,\text{N}} = 1.44 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}\)

\(r = 0.12\,\text{m}\)

(b) Coulomb forces are an action-reaction pair, so by Newton's third law the second sphere experiences a force of the same magnitude and opposite direction. Since the charges are of opposite sign the force is attractive, directed from the second sphere towards the first.

(a) \(r = 0.12\,\text{m} = 12\,\text{cm}\)
(b) \(0.2\,\text{N}\), attractive, directed towards the first sphere.

Dimensional check. Coulomb's law \(F = k e^{2}/r^{2}\) gives \([k e^{2}] = [F][L^{2}] = [\text{M L T}^{-2}][\text{L}^{2}] = [\text{M L}^{3}\,\text{T}^{-2}]\). Newton's law of gravitation \(F = G m_e m_p / r^{2}\) gives \([G m_e m_p] = [F][L^{2}] = [\text{M L}^{3}\,\text{T}^{-2}]\) as well. The two have identical dimensions, so their ratio is dimensionless.

Numerical value, using \(k = 9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2}\), \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\), \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}\), \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}\) and \(m_p = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}\):

\(k e^{2} = (9 \times 10^{9})(1.6 \times 10^{-19})^{2} = 2.304 \times 10^{-28}\,\text{N m}^{2}\)

\(G m_e m_p = (6.67 \times 10^{-11})(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(1.67 \times 10^{-27}) = 1.015 \times 10^{-67}\,\text{N m}^{2}\)

\(\dfrac{k e^{2}}{G m_e m_p} = \dfrac{2.304 \times 10^{-28}}{1.015 \times 10^{-67}} = 2.27 \times 10^{39}\)

Significance. Both forces between an electron and a proton fall off as \(1/r^{2}\), so the separation cancels in their ratio and this pure number is the ratio of the electrostatic attraction to the gravitational attraction between them, at every distance. It says the electrical force binding the hydrogen atom is roughly \(10^{39}\) times stronger than the gravitational force between the same two particles, which is why gravity is completely ignored in atomic physics while electrostatics dominates.

The ratio is dimensionless and equals \(2.3 \times 10^{39}\); it is the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between an electron and a proton.
_note: Value depends on the constants used; computed with k = 9e9, e = 1.6e-19, G = 6.67e-11, m_e = 9.11e-31 kg, m_p = 1.67e-27 kg.

solution:
(a) To say that charge is quantised means that the charge on any body is never an arbitrary quantity but always an integral multiple of one indivisible elementary charge \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\), that is

\(q = n e, \qquad n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \ldots\)

The physical reason is that a body is charged only by gaining or losing whole electrons; half an electron cannot be transferred. So charge exists in discrete packets of size \(e\), and a value such as \(2.5\,e\) is impossible.

(b) Because \(e\) is minute compared with the charges handled in the laboratory, the step between one allowed value and the next is far too small to detect. A charge of \(1\,\mu\text{C}\) already corresponds to

\(n = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{C}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 6.25 \times 10^{12}\)

electrons, so adding or removing a single electron alters the charge by about one part in \(10^{13}\), which no instrument can resolve. The graininess is therefore invisible at the macroscopic scale and charge behaves as though it varied continuously, exactly as sand poured from a bucket looks like a smooth stream even though it is made of separate grains.

(a) Charge is quantised: every charge is \(q = ne\) with \(n\) an integer and \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\), because charging transfers whole electrons.
(b) Macroscopic charges correspond to \(n \sim 10^{12}\text{--}10^{13}\) electrons, so the elementary step \(e\) is negligible compared with the charge itself and the quantisation cannot be detected; charge may be treated as continuous.

Rubbing does not create charge out of nothing; it only redistributes charge that was already there. Glass and silk are initially neutral, meaning each contains exactly as much positive charge on its nuclei as negative charge on its electrons. When the two are rubbed together the intimate contact lets some loosely bound electrons cross from the glass to the silk, because silk holds electrons more strongly than glass does.

The glass, having lost \(n\) electrons, is left with an excess positive charge \(+ne\); the silk, having gained the very same \(n\) electrons, acquires an equal negative charge \(-ne\). The two charges are therefore always equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, and the total charge of the glass-plus-silk system is

\(q_{\text{total}} = (+ne) + (-ne) = 0\)

exactly what it was before rubbing. No charge has been produced or destroyed, so the law of conservation of charge is obeyed.

This is why the phenomenon is seen for many other pairs of bodies as well, and why the two members of a pair always end up oppositely charged: which body becomes positive depends on which of the two grips electrons more tightly, but whatever crosses from one is exactly what arrives at the other. If charge could be created, the two bodies could be charged independently, or one could be charged without the other; that is never observed.

The charges appearing on the glass and the silk are equal and opposite, arising purely from a transfer of electrons from one body to the other, so the net charge of the isolated system remains zero throughout. Charge is redistributed, never created or destroyed, which is precisely the law of conservation of charge.

Let the square ABCD have side \(a = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\) and let O be its centre, where the charge \(q = 1\,\mu\text{C}\) is placed. In the square ABCD the vertices A and C are the ends of one diagonal, and B and D the ends of the other, so O is the midpoint of both diagonals and every corner is the same distance

\(r = \dfrac{a\sqrt{2}}{2} = \dfrac{(0.10\,\text{m})(1.414)}{2} = 0.0707\,\text{m}\)

from O.

Charges at A and C. Both equal \(2\,\mu\text{C}\) and both lie at the same distance \(r\) from O, so each exerts a force of the same magnitude \(F_{AC} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2\,\mu\text{C})q}{r^{2}}\) on the central charge. But A and C are on opposite sides of O along the diagonal AC, so the two forces act along the same line in exactly opposite directions and cancel.

Charges at B and D. Both equal \(-5\,\mu\text{C}\) and are again equidistant from O and diametrically opposite along the diagonal BD, so those two forces are likewise equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and they cancel too.

Since both pairs cancel independently, the resultant of all four is zero. Note the result does not depend on the size of the charges or on the side of the square, only on the diagonal symmetry of the arrangement.

The net force on the \(1\,\mu\text{C}\) charge at the centre is zero.

(a) The polythene carries a negative charge, so it has gained electrons; rubbing transferred electrons from the wool to the polythene. Since charge is quantised, \(|q| = n e\), so

\(n = \dfrac{|q|}{e} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}} = 1.875 \times 10^{12}\)

about \(1.9 \times 10^{12}\) electrons, transferred from the wool to the polythene.

(b) Yes. An electron carries mass as well as charge, so moving electrons necessarily moves mass. The polythene gains, and the wool loses,

\(\Delta m = n\,m_e = (1.875 \times 10^{12})(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}) = 1.71 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{kg}\)

So mass is transferred from wool to polythene, but the amount is about \(10^{-18}\,\text{kg}\), utterly negligible compared with the mass of either body and far below the sensitivity of any balance.

(a) \(n = 1.9 \times 10^{12}\) electrons, transferred from the wool to the polythene.
(b) Yes, mass is transferred from wool to polythene, \(\Delta m = 1.7 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{kg}\), which is negligible.

(a) Converting the separation to SI units, \(r = 50\,\text{cm} = 0.50\,\text{m}\). The radii are negligible compared with \(r\), so the spheres may be treated as point charges and Coulomb's law applies with \(q_1 = q_2 = q = 6.5 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C}\):

\(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q^{2}}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N m}^{2}\,\text{C}^{-2})(6.5 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{C})^{2}}{(0.50\,\text{m})^{2}} = \dfrac{3.80 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{N m}^{2}}{0.25\,\text{m}^{2}}\)

\(F = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\)

(b) Now each charge is \(2q\) and the separation is \(r/2\), so

\(F' = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(2q)(2q)}{(r/2)^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{4q^{2}}{r^{2}/4} = 16\,\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q^{2}}{r^{2}} = 16F\)

Doubling each charge multiplies the force by \(4\) and halving the distance multiplies it by a further \(4\), giving a factor of \(16\) in all:

\(F' = 16 \times (1.521 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}) = 0.243\,\text{N}\)

(a) \(F = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\), repulsive.
(b) \(F' = 16F = 0.24\,\text{N}\), repulsive.
